- The background is the dominant color.
- Each panel contains exactly one non-background foreground color.

Rule
- Align the left and right panels by row and column.
- A cell in the output is grey iff both aligned panel cells are background.
- All other output cells are background.

Key insight
- The output is not the union or intersection of the colored objects; it is the
  complement of their overlaid occupancy mask.

annotation.src: aligned cell pairs from the two equal side-by-side panels
annotation.transform: output grey where both aligned cells are background; output background everywhere else
annotation.grid_shape: same height and half the input width

references.docstring:
Crop each foreground sprite to its bounding box and pack the crops tightly along the sprites' layout axis.

Input structure:
- The input is a background grid containing multiple separated, monochrome, 8-connected sprites.
- The sprites all have the same bounding-box shape.
- The sprite centers are spread more in either rows or columns, defining a vertical or horizontal layout.

Rule:
- Extract each sprite's bbox crop.
- If the sprite centers span more columns than rows, order sprites left-to-right and concatenate the crops horizontally.
- Otherwise, order sprites top-to-bottom and concatenate the crops vertically.

Key insight:
- The output is not a recoloring; it is the same sprites with all empty space between their bboxes removed.

annotation.src: 8-connected monochrome foreground sprites s with equal bbox shape, ordered along the larger spread axis
annotation.dst: tightly packed output slots d in the same horizontal or vertical order
annotation.match_cond: rank(s left-to-right for horizontal layouts, or top-to-bottom for vertical layouts) == rank(d)
annotation.transform: crop each s to its bbox and paste the crops unchanged with all inter-sprite background spacing removed
annotation.grid_shape: one sprite bbox tall by N bbox widths for horizontal layouts, or N bbox heights by one sprite bbox wide for vertical layouts

references.docstring:
Return the values hidden under the solid marker rectangle by reflecting them from the bilaterally symmetric grid.

Input structure
- The input scene has horizontal and vertical mirror symmetry except for one solid rectangular marker mask.
- The marker color appears only as that solid rectangle.
- The requested output has the same shape as the marker rectangle.

Rule
- Identify the unique solid marker rectangle whose horizontal, vertical, and 180-degree mirror counterparts reveal consistent non-marker values.
- For each marker pixel, copy the unique visible value from its reflected counterparts into the corresponding output cell.

Key insight
- The marker hides a rectangular patch of a bilaterally symmetric image; the missing value for each covered cell is visible at its mirror locations.

annotation.src: solid rectangular marker over a horizontally and vertically mirrored color pattern
annotation.dst: hidden marker-sized rectangle
annotation.transform: for each marker pixel, copy the unique non-marker color visible at its horizontal, vertical, or 180-degree reflection counterpart
annotation.grid_shape: output is the marker bbox crop

references.docstring:
Move each rectangular object into the matching platform gap, rotating it so its two-cell side is vertical.

Input structure
- The last row is a solid non-background platform color.
- The row above the platform contains only background and platform-color separator runs; background gaps between consecutive separator runs are slots.
- Every non-background, non-platform object above the shelf is a solid monochrome rectangle with one side of length two.

Rule
- Clear those source rectangles from their original locations.
- Rotate a rectangle if needed so it is two rows tall.
- Place each normalized rectangle bottom-aligned with the shelf row inside the unique slot whose width matches the rectangle's normalized width.

Key insight
- The platform separators encode target slot widths, while each source rectangle's non-two dimension encodes the slot it belongs in.

annotation.src: solid monochrome foreground rectangle s above the platform, excluding bg and platform color
annotation.dst: background gap slot d between consecutive platform-color separator runs in the row above the solid platform
annotation.match_cond: width(orient s with its length-2 side vertical) == width(d)
annotation.transform: clear s from its original location; rotate if needed to make s two rows tall, then place it bottom-aligned in d

references.docstring:
Compress the sparse lattice by deleting the all-background separator rows and columns.

Input structure
- The grid has even height and width.
- Every odd-indexed row and every odd-indexed column is background.
- The meaningful colored pixels occupy the even-row/even-column lattice positions.

Rule
- Keep the cells at even row and even column indices, preserving their colors.
- The output height and width are half of the input height and width.

Key insight
- The odd rows and columns are separators between logical cells; removing them reveals the compact symbol grid.

annotation.src: foreground pixels on a background lattice where every odd row and odd column is a separator
annotation.transform: delete the separator rows and columns; preserve the colors at the remaining even-row/even-column cells
annotation.grid_shape: half the input height and half the input width

references.docstring:
Paint yellow the background cells on the unobstructed shortest monotone corridor between two doorway frames.

Input structure
- The grid has a background, two small frame objects in one foreground color, and one center marker in each frame.
- Each marker has exactly one background 4-neighbor, the doorway gap; the next cell outward is the exterior doorway cell.

Rule
- Treat all existing foreground cells as blockers.
- Between the two exterior doorway cells, allow only row/column steps that move toward the other exterior cell.
- Paint every background cell that lies on some such path from one exterior cell to the other, plus the two doorway gaps, yellow.

Key insight
- The output is not a single chosen route: it is the union of all shortest monotone paths that can pass between the two frames.

annotation.src: one exterior cell just outside a grey-marker doorway in a small frame object
annotation.dst: the other exterior cell just outside the second grey-marker doorway
annotation.path: all shortest monotone 4-neighbor paths from s to d, stepping only toward d and avoiding existing foreground frame/marker pixels
annotation.trajectory: paint every background pixel that lies on at least one valid path yellow
annotation.transform: also paint the two doorway gap pixels yellow; keep all frame and marker pixels unchanged

references.docstring:
Draw a fixed 15x15 lattice whose separator spacing is set by the input square size.

Input structure
The input is a non-black solid square: every pixel has the same foreground
color, and the side length of that square is the lattice cell size.

Rule
Create a black 15x15 output. Starting after one input-side-length block,
paint full rows and columns in the input color every side_length + 1 cells.

Key insight
The input's content supplies only two parameters: the visible color and the
spacing between lattice separator lines.

annotation.src: solid single-color square; its side length n and color c define the lattice
annotation.transform: create a black 15x15 grid and paint full rows and columns with c at indices n, 2n+1, 3n+2, ... while in bounds
annotation.grid_shape: fixed 15x15

references.docstring:
Extend each path object to its matched marker and recolor an equal-length tail from the path's opposite endpoint.

Input structure
- The background is the dominant color.
- Non-background pixels form the same number of isolated marker pixels and 4-connected monochrome path objects.
- Each path object is a one-pixel-wide, unbranched orthogonal path with exactly two endpoints.
- Every marker has a clear row or column sightline to at least one path endpoint, and the global marker-to-path assignment is unique.

Rule
- Match markers to path objects by the unique one-to-one assignment where each marker sees its object's endpoint along a straight background gap.
- Fill that gap with the matched path object's color, leaving the marker pixel itself unchanged.
- From the opposite endpoint of the same path, recolor as many existing path cells with the marker color as there were gap cells.

Key insight
- The marker does not simply color the nearby endpoint; its distance from the path measures how much of the far end of that path is converted.

annotation.src: isolated marker pixel s
annotation.dst: one-pixel-wide unbranched path object d
annotation.match_cond: s has a clear horizontal or vertical bg sightline to an endpoint of d; assignment is the unique one-to-one matching
annotation.transform: paint the sightline gap with d.color; from d's opposite endpoint, recolor len(gap) path cells with s.color; keep marker pixels unchanged

references.docstring:
Extend the bottom source as a two-cell diagonal band upward-right, sliding it right around foreground blockers.

Input structure
- The grid has a dominant background color.
- Exactly one foreground pixel lies on the bottom row; this is the colored source.
- Any other foreground pixels are blockers that remain fixed.

Rule
- Copy the input, then emit the source color upward one row at a time.
- The first row above the source starts a two-cell horizontal band at the source column; each next row shifts that band one column right.
- If the band would touch a blocker in its row, shift it further right until both band cells avoid blockers.
- When such an extra shift leaves a gap from the previous row's band, fill the gap on the previous row with the source color.
- Stop when the band has moved completely past the right edge.

Key insight
- Blockers do not stop the diagonal ray; they push the two-cell-wide band right, and the previous row is widened only enough to keep the trail connected.

annotation.src: unique bottom-row foreground source pixel; all other foreground pixels are fixed blockers
annotation.path: diagonal upward-right row sweep: the first two-cell band starts at the source column, each next row normally shifts one column right, and any blocker hit shifts the band further right until clear; stop after the band passes the right edge
annotation.trajectory: paint source color on the band cells, clipped by the right edge; when an extra right shift creates a gap, fill that gap on the previous row
annotation.transform: preserve the source pixel and all blocker pixels

references.docstring:
Composite three stacked same-size panels into one panel, with the bottom panel painted last.

Input structure
- The input is three equal-height panels stacked vertically on a common background.
- Each panel contains exactly one foreground color.
- Corresponding cells across the three panels occupy the same output position.

Rule
- Start with the middle panel as the base.
- Copy every non-background pixel from the top panel onto the same position.
- Copy every non-background pixel from the bottom panel onto the same position, overwriting both earlier layers.

Key insight
- Cell conflicts are resolved by panel position/layer role: middle first, then top, then bottom, not by numeric color order.

annotation.src: three equal-size single-color foreground masks stacked vertically on a black background
annotation.transform: compose corresponding cells into one panel: middle panel is the base, top panel overwrites non-background cells, and bottom panel overwrites both
annotation.grid_shape: same height and width as one stacked panel

references.docstring:
Slide every colored domino straight toward the full red edge wall until it is blocked.

Input structure
- The background is empty space.
- One non-background color forms a complete one-cell-thick edge wall and appears nowhere else.
- Every other foreground object is a monochromatic 4-connected domino, either horizontal or vertical.

Rule
- Keep the edge wall fixed and clear the other foreground objects from their original positions.
- The wall side gives the gravity direction: objects move up, down, left, or right toward that wall.
- Settle dominoes nearest the wall first; each domino slides rigidly along the gravity direction until the next step would hit the wall, another settled domino, or the grid boundary.

Key insight
- The full edge wall is the only anchor; the output is the gravity-packed state of all remaining dominoes against that wall.

annotation.src: each non-wall monochrome domino object s
annotation.path: straight toward the complete red edge wall, perpendicular to that edge, stopping when the next step would hit the wall, a settled domino, or the grid boundary
annotation.trajectory: move s rigidly to its stopped endpoint, preserving shape and color
annotation.transform: clear s.old cells to background; keep the red edge wall unchanged
annotation.multi_step: settle dominoes nearest the wall first so farther dominoes stack behind them

references.docstring:
Recolor the grey object with the color of the marker set closest to it, erasing all markers.

Input structure
- The grid has a black background with one 4-connected grey object.
- Every other foreground color appears as one or more isolated marker pixels.

Rule
- For each marker color, measure the smallest squared Euclidean distance from any marker pixel of that color to any grey-object pixel.
- The unique marker color with the smallest such distance becomes the output color.
- Return a blank background grid with the grey object's mask painted in that selected color.

Key insight
- The scattered pixels are competing color labels; only the label with the closest approach to the grey object survives.

annotation.src: candidate marker color sets s, each made of isolated non-grey foreground pixels
annotation.dst: the single grey object d
annotation.match_cond: s has the unique smallest squared Euclidean distance from any marker pixel in s to any pixel of d
annotation.transform: erase all markers and recolor d with s.color on the black background

references.docstring:
Invert the single-color 3x3 mask, turning marked cells black and unmarked cells into the marker color's paired color.

Input structure:
- The grid is 3x3.
- Black cells form the background; every non-black cell has the same foreground color.
- The foreground color is one of the trained paired colors: teal, green, or grey.

Rule:
- Choose the paired fill color for the foreground: teal -> red, green -> blue, grey -> yellow.
- Paint every black input cell with that paired color.
- Paint every foreground input cell black.

Key insight:
- Geometry only selects which cells swap roles; the output color is determined by the foreground color's visible pair.

annotation.src: 3x3 grid with black background cells and exactly one foreground color from the paired set: teal, green, or grey
annotation.transform: erase the foreground mask to black; recolor every black background cell to the paired output color: teal -> red, green -> blue, grey -> yellow

references.docstring:
Reflect the red shape across its touched vertical edge into a teal-and-black negative half.

Input structure
The input is a black grid containing red foreground pixels. The foreground
touches exactly one vertical border, and that border is the reflection seam.

Rule
Horizontally reflect the input. In the reflected half, turn black pixels
teal and all red foreground pixels black. If the red foreground touches the
left border, place the reflected half on the left and the original on the
right; if it touches the right border, place the original on the left and
the reflected half on the right.

Key insight
The output is the original grid joined to a color-remapped mirror image
across the single vertical edge touched by the red foreground.

annotation.src: black grid with a red foreground mask touching exactly one vertical border
annotation.transform: mirror the input across the touched vertical border; in the mirrored half recolor black pixels teal and red pixels black, then concatenate it on the seam side
annotation.grid_shape: same height and twice the input width

references.docstring:
Summarize a foreground line partition as a plain background-colored grid whose shape is the number of row and column regions.

Input structure
The input has one background color and one foreground color; the foreground
pixels are exactly the union of complete horizontal and vertical separator
lines, possibly including a line on the border.
Rule
Count the contiguous runs of non-separator rows and non-separator columns.
Return a uniform grid of the background color with those run counts as its
height and width.
Key insight
The output does not preserve the separator lines themselves; it records only
how many background regions the line partition creates in each direction.

annotation.src: two-color board divided by complete one-pixel foreground separator rows and columns
annotation.transform: replace each contiguous background row band and column band by one output pixel; fill every output pixel with the input background color
annotation.grid_shape: number of non-separator row bands x number of non-separator column bands

references.docstring:
Extend each non-background pixel into an L reaching the nearest vertical and horizontal grid edges.

Input structure
A mostly background grid contains one or more isolated foreground marker pixels.
Each marker is closer to one vertical edge and one horizontal edge, with no midpoint ties.

Rule
For every marker at (r, c), draw its color along column c from the marker to the nearer
top or bottom edge, and along row r from the marker to the nearer left or right edge.

Key insight
Each single pixel is the corner of an edge-facing L; its directions are chosen by nearest
grid-boundary distance rather than by color identity.

annotation.src: isolated non-background marker pixels s
annotation.path: from each s, one straight ray along s.column to the nearer top/bottom grid edge and one straight ray along s.row to the nearer left/right grid edge
annotation.trajectory: paint every cell on both rays with s.color, including s
annotation.transform: keep all markers and combine the independently painted L shapes on the same canvas

references.docstring:
Grow each red control pixel upward through black space, sidestepping right under gray blockers.

Input structure
- The background is black.
- Red pixels are control pixels on the bottom row.
- The only other foreground color is the obstacle color.

Rule
- From each red control pixel, repeatedly try to move one cell upward.
- If the cell above is background, paint it red and continue from there.
- If the cell above is an obstacle, step one cell right on the current row
  and paint that background cell red; if that right cell is unavailable or
  not background, stop that path.

Key insight
- The red output is not a set of fixed columns: each bottom control emits an
  upward path whose turns are caused locally by gray cells directly above it.

annotation.src: red control pixels on the bottom row
annotation.path: move upward through black cells; when the cell above is grey, step one cell right on the current row if that cell is black, otherwise stop
annotation.trajectory: paint every black cell visited by the path red
annotation.transform: leave grey obstacles and the original red controls unchanged

references.docstring:
Extend the given seed color cycle across the middle row at triangular-number column positions.

Input structure
The grid has three rows with a dominant background color. All foreground
pixels lie on one row, and their columns are the initial triangular sequence
0, 1, 3, 6, ...

Rule
Read the foreground colors from left to right as a repeating cycle. Starting
from a background grid of the same shape, write that color cycle at every
triangular column that fits within the width.

Key insight
The increasing gaps between active columns are 1, 2, 3, 4, ...; the input
supplies only the first colors of the cycle, and the missing triangular
positions continue the same cycle.

annotation.src: foreground seed colors on the middle row at the first triangular columns 0, 1, 3, ...
annotation.dst: all triangular columns on the same row within the grid width
annotation.transform: repeat the seed colors cyclically at those columns and leave every other pixel as background

references.docstring:
Copy each red or teal marker upward from the blue row and connect it back with blue cells.

Input structure
- The background is the dominant empty color.
- All foreground pixels lie in one full-width horizontal row.
- That row is blue except for red and/or teal marker pixels.

Rule
- A red marker is copied four rows above itself; a teal marker is copied three rows above itself.
- Fill the intervening cells in the same column with blue, leaving the original row unchanged.

Key insight
- The marker color encodes the upward distance of the vertical stem.

annotation.src: red and teal marker pixels embedded in the full-width blue row
annotation.path: vertical ray upward in the marker's column, four rows for red markers and three rows for teal markers
annotation.trajectory: copy the marker color at the top of the ray and paint the intervening cells blue
annotation.transform: leave the original row and all other background cells unchanged

references.docstring:
Recover the original quadrant from a four-way mirrored rectangular panel.

Input structure
- The input is a larger background grid containing one foreground panel.
- The panel has even height and width.
- Its four quadrants are reflections of the same source pattern.

Rule
- Crop to the foreground panel's bounding box.
- Read the upper-left quadrant as the source pattern.
- Verify that the other quadrants are its left-right, up-down, and 180-degree reflections.

Key insight
- The apparent 12x12 drawing is not a pixel-scale zoom; it is a reflected 2x2 mosaic whose upper-left quadrant is the requested 4x4 image.

annotation.src: foreground panel formed as a 2x2 mosaic of reflected quadrants
annotation.transform: crop to the foreground bbox and output the upper-left quadrant after verifying the other quadrants are its horizontal, vertical, and 180-degree reflections
annotation.grid_shape: half the cropped panel height by half the cropped panel width

references.docstring:
Move each non-bar foreground pixel one row downward, and splash diagonal rays upward when it lands directly above the bar.

Input structure
- The background is the dominant color.
- One foreground color forms a single full-width horizontal bar.
- The only other foreground color appears as isolated moving pixels off the bar.

Rule
- Clear the moving pixels from their original locations and paint each one at the same column one row lower.
- If a moved pixel lands immediately above the horizontal bar, also paint both upward diagonals from that landing pixel until they leave the grid.
- The full-width bar and all background cells outside those shifted/splashed paths remain unchanged.

Key insight
- The bar is a trigger line: pixels always shift down one step, but only pixels that become adjacent to the bar emit the diagonal splash.

annotation.src: non-bar foreground pixels
annotation.path: one-step downward shift; if the shifted pixel is immediately above the full-width bar, emit both upward diagonal rays from that landing cell until the grid boundary
annotation.trajectory: erase original source pixels and paint shifted and splashed positions with the source color
annotation.transform: preserve the full-width bar and all other background cells

references.docstring:
Crop the unique foreground object whose mask is not mirror-symmetric left-to-right.

Input structure
- A dominant background surrounds several same-color 8-connected foreground objects.
- Exactly one foreground color appears.
- All but one foreground object are mirror-symmetric left-to-right inside their tight bboxes.

Rule
- Split the non-background pixels into 8-connected objects.
- Build each object's tight bbox crop over the background.
- Return the single crop whose foreground mask differs from its left-right reflection.

Key insight
- The input is a set of candidate sprites, and vertical-axis asymmetry identifies which one to extract regardless of color or position.

annotation.src: 8-connected same-color foreground objects on the dominant background
annotation.transform: select the unique object whose tight-bbox mask is not mirror-symmetric left-to-right and render only that object
annotation.grid_shape: tight bbox crop of the selected object

references.docstring:
Paint the even square-distance rings around the solid foreground cross yellow.

Input structure:
- The grid has one background color and one foreground color.
- The foreground is exactly one full row and one full column crossing each other.
- Yellow is absent from the input and is the output fill color.

Rule:
- Locate the unique solid foreground row and column, whose intersection is the ring center.
- For every background pixel, compute its Chebyshev distance from that center.
- Recolor background pixels with even Chebyshev distance to yellow.
- Keep the foreground cross unchanged.

Key insight:
- The output is not drawn from separate quadrant patterns; it is one set of alternating square rings centered on the cross intersection.

annotation.src: background pixels around a single solid foreground row/column cross
annotation.transform: recolor to yellow each background pixel whose Chebyshev distance from the cross intersection is even; preserve the foreground cross and odd-distance background pixels

references.docstring:
Expand the left-edge 2x2 motif into rightward copies scaled by powers of two.

Input structure
- The background is the most common color.
- The only foreground pixels form a filled 2x2 motif in columns 0 and 1.
Rule
- Start with a background-filled output of the same shape.
- For scales 1, 2, 4, ... that fit horizontally, stamp the motif scaled by that factor.
- Place each scaled stamp at column 2 * (scale - 1), with its top row band ending on the
  original motif's top row and its bottom row band starting on the original motif's bottom row.
Key insight
- The original 2x2 motif is the smallest copy in a dyadic sequence: each next copy doubles
  both dimensions, starts immediately to the right, and grows away from the seam between
  the motif's two rows.

annotation.summary: Repeat the left-edge 2x2 motif as rightward power-of-two scaled copies.
annotation.src: filled 2x2 foreground motif in the first two columns
annotation.dst: rightward power-of-two scaled copy positions on the same grid
annotation.transform: clear to background, then for scales 1, 2, 4, ... that fit horizontally, stamp the motif scaled by that factor at column 2*(scale-1), vertically centered on the seam so the top motif row grows upward and the bottom motif row grows downward

references.docstring:
Fill the gap on the longer edge-bar side in the columns where the two edge bars overlap.

Input structure
- The grid has a black dominant background.
- One non-background internal row is a full-width red separator.
- The first and last rows each contain one contiguous horizontal bar of the same non-red color.

Rule
- Find the column sets occupied by the top and bottom edge bars.
- Compute their column overlap.
- If the top bar is longer, paint yellow through the overlap columns from below the top row down to the separator.
- If the bottom bar is longer, paint yellow through the overlap columns from below the separator down to above the bottom row.
- Leave all original non-background pixels unchanged.

Key insight
- The side to fill is chosen by the longer edge bar, while the fill width comes from the shared horizontal projection of both bars.

annotation.src: same-color top and bottom edge bars on a black background, separated by one full-width red row
annotation.transform: compute the overlap of the two bar column sets; on the side whose edge bar is longer, paint yellow in those overlap columns between the edge row and the red separator; leave all other pixels unchanged

references.docstring:
Use the red divider as a wall: fill the 4-connected lower-left side with the single payload color and clear the other side to black.

Input structure
- The grid contains black cells, red divider pixels, and exactly one other payload color.
- Treating red as blocked, all non-red pixels form exactly two 4-connected regions.
- The lower-left corner is part of the region to fill.

Rule
- Preserve every red pixel.
- Fill every non-red pixel in the same 4-connected region as the lower-left corner with the payload color.
- Recolor the other non-red region to black.

Key insight
The noisy black/payload pattern in each region is irrelevant; the red wall partitions the canvas, and the side anchored at the lower-left corner is the solid foreground side.

annotation.src: black/payload pixels partitioned into two 4-connected regions by red divider pixels
annotation.transform: preserve red pixels; fill the region containing the lower-left corner with the payload color and recolor the other non-red region to black

references.docstring:
Complete every magenta-marked transformed copy of the yellow/magenta template by painting the missing yellow cells.

Input structure
- The existing yellow pixels all lie inside one small rectangular template region.
- That template region is fully tiled by yellow and magenta pixels.
- Elsewhere, magenta pixels mark incomplete rotated or reflected copies of the same two-color template.

Rule
- Extract the template from the bounding box of all yellow pixels.
- For every rotated or reflected template placement whose magenta cells are all visible magenta pixels, paint each visible non-magenta yellow-template cell yellow.
- Allow yellow-template cells to be clipped off the grid edge, but require every magenta-template cell to be inside the grid.

Key insight
- The magenta cells are the alignment signature for each oriented copy; the yellow part of the same template is what must be restored.

annotation.src: yellow/magenta rectangular template sprite s, including all rotated/reflected variants
annotation.dst: candidate grid placement d anchored by magenta pixels
annotation.match_cond: s.magenta mask is entirely in-bounds and equals magenta pixels at d; s.yellow cells may be clipped by the grid edge but cannot cover magenta
annotation.transform: paint every visible cell of the matched s.yellow mask yellow; keep all other cells unchanged

references.docstring:
Build a larger square from the input grid and its three quarter-turn rotations.

Input structure
A square grid whose whole contents form the pattern; there is no separate
background object or marker.

Rule
Make a 2n by 2n output from four n by n quadrants: the original grid in the
upper-left, the grid rotated 90 degrees counterclockwise in the upper-right,
the grid rotated 180 degrees in the lower-left, and the grid rotated 270
degrees counterclockwise in the lower-right.

Key insight
The output repeats the entire input under rotation, so every input cell
appears once in each quadrant rather than being expanded in place.

annotation.summary: Arrange the input square and its three quarter-turn rotations into a doubled square.
annotation.src: entire n x n input grid
annotation.dst: 2x2 grid of n x n quadrants
annotation.transform: place the original grid in the upper-left, its 90-degree counterclockwise rotation in the upper-right, its 180-degree rotation in the lower-left, and its 270-degree counterclockwise rotation in the lower-right
annotation.grid_shape: input height and width doubled

references.docstring:
Extend each left-edge beam marker rightward, letting obstacle pixels create side wakes and split branches.

Input structure
- The grid has a dominant background, one seed color whose pixels all lie in the leftmost column, and one obstacle color.
- Seed pixels are horizontal emitters; all other non-background pixels are fixed one-pixel obstacles.
- Obstacles may appear on a beam row or immediately diagonally in front of another obstacle.

Rule
- From every seed, paint background cells to the right with the seed color.
- When a beam hits an obstacle, keep the obstacle unchanged and paint the available three-cell side wakes above and below it.
- A side wake is blocked if its left entry cell is an unactivated obstacle; obstacles reached inside wakes paint only their open side wakes and the cell immediately to their right.
- If a hit obstacle has obstacles at both forward diagonals, the original beam stops and full beams continue on those two adjacent rows without painting back through the parent obstacle.

Key insight
- The output is a directed ray simulation: obstacle pixels are fixed blockers that locally thicken the beam, and paired forward-diagonal blockers are the only places where the beam splits into new horizontal paths.

annotation.src: left-edge seed pixels s in the unique seed color
annotation.path: horizontal rays to the right; a hit obstacle paints open side wakes, and if obstacles occupy both forward diagonals the ray stops and branches rightward on the two adjacent rows
annotation.trajectory: paint reached background pixels with s.color
annotation.transform: keep all original seed and obstacle pixels unchanged; side-wake entry is blocked by an unactivated obstacle and split branches cannot paint back through their parent obstacle
annotation.multi_step: simulate rays left-to-right from each seed; obstacles reached inside wakes activate locally but do not become full beams unless created by a two-forward-diagonal split

references.docstring:
Copy the solid foreground rectangle that has the fewest internal marker pixels.

Input structure
- The input has a background and several separated 4-connected foreground rectangles.
- Each rectangle is mostly one fill color, with marker pixels of other foreground colors.

Rule
- Crop every solid foreground rectangle.
- Count a rectangle's markers as the pixels that differ from its unique dominant fill color.
- Return the crop of the single rectangle with the smallest marker count.

Key insight
- The wanted object is selected by marker sparsity, not by size, position, or marker color.

annotation.src: 4-connected solid foreground rectangles with dominant fill color and internal marker pixels
annotation.transform: crop the single rectangle with the fewest marker pixels, where markers are pixels not matching that rectangle's dominant fill color
annotation.grid_shape: tight bbox crop of the selected rectangle

references.docstring:
Fill each background chamber with the majority color of the colored marker pixels touching it.

references.docstring:

- If that orange pixel roofs a one-cell notch, paint the vertical approach red and put a new marker in the notch below it.
- Otherwise recolor the hit orange pixel teal, mark the cell below it yellow, draw red under the rest of its rightward row-run, mark the exit cell green, and continue upward from that exit column.
- If no orange pixel remains above the current column, paint red up to the top edge and put a new marker on the top edge.

Key insight
- The route is a deterministic upward scan on the original orange mask; each exposed hit exits just to the right of the contiguous orange run on that row.

annotation.path: climb upward in the current column to the nearest orange pixel; after each exposed hit, turn right under the contiguous orange run and continue from the right exit; stop in the notch below an orange roof, or at the top edge if no orange remains above
annotation.trajectory: paint the vertical approach and horizontal under-run route red
annotation.dst: terminal top-edge cell or notch cell below the blocking orange roof
annotation.transform: passed orange hit pixels become teal; the cell below a hit becomes yellow and the right exit cell becomes green; place a marker at the terminal cell and keep all other pixels unchanged

references.docstring:

For each green marker that acts as a wedge tip, find the two diagonal side
rays in one of the four orientations.  The side rays must contain green
clues at a shared distance from the tip.  The wedge height is the farthest
shared clue distance, extended by any contiguous green clue run from the tip.
Paint every non-green pixel inside the resulting triangular wedge teal.

Key insight
The green pixels are not objects to move; they are sparse boundary clues for
45-degree triangular fill regions, and unrelated far-away diagonal markers
are ignored unless they are part of a shared-distance clue or near-tip run.

annotation.transform: fill each indicated triangular wedge with teal while preserving the green marker pixels; distant diagonal markers only extend a wedge when supported by shared-distance clues or a contiguous side run

references.docstring:

- The cell regions form a complete rectangular array with at least three rows and three columns.

- Preserve every lattice pixel.
- For each cell region, recolor it red if its region-row or region-column is on the outer edge of the array.
- Recolor all strictly interior cell regions green.

Key insight:
- The black cells are not independent pixels; they are the holes of a larger lattice, and their array position determines the fill color.

annotation.transform: preserve the lattice; recolor cell regions on the outer row or column of the region array red and strictly interior regions green

- The 9x9 grid is a doubled 5x5 node lattice: even-even cells are nodes, and the colored

annotation.path: on a 5x5 output lattice, center the square spiral at node (2*s.row, 2*s.col); trace outward with step lengths 1, 1, 2, 2, ... in up, right, down, left order, clipping steps whose endpoint leaves the lattice
annotation.trajectory: paint every lattice node and the midpoint pixel of each retained adjacent-node step with s.color
annotation.transform: use the input background color for all non-painted output pixels

annotation.match_cond: left-to-right rank of s == top-to-bottom rank of d
annotation.transform: count each object's enclosed black pixels not 4-connected to its bbox border, then fill that many cells left-to-right in its row block with the object color

references.docstring:

immediately above that separator, and exactly one non-background seed pixel
below it whose color is the first code entry.

Read the code row from the left edge through its last non-background entry,
preserving any background entries inside that span as blank ring colors.  A

lower singleton only supplies the center of that expansion.

references.docstring:

The right-panel objects are not copied by position; their shapes are a palette
that names which color belongs in each matching left-panel hole.

inside its bounding rectangle and also paint their reflected copies: wide
frames reflect left/right, while tall frames reflect top/bottom. Clear all

The outside pixels are not copied into the output; their relative layout is an orientation legend for
the matching singleton colors embedded in the rectangle.

references.docstring:

Input structure:

- The frame has an even-height and even-width empty interior.

- A marker in the northeast or southwest side supplies the other two quadrants.

references.docstring:
Erase the color-bar legend and complete the vertical stack by copying the shared sprite mask into every ordered color slot.

Input structure
The grid has a black background, one solid rectangular legend made of
adjacent vertical color bars, and one or more placed instances of the same
sprite mask in colors from that legend.

Read the legend colors from left to right.  These colors fill consecutive
vertical sprite slots from top to bottom.  The existing sprite instances
provide the common mask, left edge, and vertical anchor of the stack; missing
legend colors are inserted into their corresponding slots.

Existing sprites are already in the same rank positions named by the legend,
so any one of them fixes the whole ordered stack geometry.

references.docstring:
Reconstruct the clean lattice and put the marker color at every separator-row/column intersection.

Input structure

- Clear all noisy marker pixels that are not at separator intersections.
- Repaint every separator row and column with the lattice color.
- Paint every separator-row/column intersection with the marker color.

- The invariant separator rows and columns are the complete non-background
  rows/columns; scattered marker pixels are noise except where these lines cross.

references.docstring:
Reflect the multi-cell foreground mask across each singleton marker so the marker becomes one cell of its colored copy.

Input structure
A background canvas contains one multi-pixel foreground object and one or more singleton marker colors. Each marker
shares exactly one row or exactly one column with a pixel of the source object.

Rule
Keep the source object. For each marker, if it shares a row with exactly one source pixel, reflect the whole source
object horizontally through the vertical midline between that source pixel and the marker. If it shares a column
with exactly one source pixel, reflect the whole source object vertically through the horizontal midline between
them. Paint the reflected mask in the marker color.

The singleton marker is one already-reflected cell of the source object, so its aligned source pixel fixes the
mirror axis for the entire copy.

annotation.dst: reflected footprint of s through the axis midway between each marker and its aligned source pixel

references.docstring:
Draw the red trace from its border marker, detouring around each blue/green bar it hits.

Input structure

- The red marker travels straight inward from its border.
- When the trace hits a blue bar, it passes around the bar on the left side
  relative to its direction of travel.
- When the trace hits a green bar, it passes around the bar on the right
  side relative to its direction of travel.
- Existing bars are preserved; only background cells on the trace become red.

Key insight
- The trace keeps the same overall forward direction; each hit bar only
  shifts the current lane by forcing a detour one cell before the obstacle.

annotation.path: straight inward ray from s; whenever the ray first hits a perpendicular blue/green bar, turn one cell before it and pass just outside the bar: blue chooses the left side relative to travel, green chooses the right side; then resume the same inward direction from the shifted lane until the boundary

references.docstring:
Expand each marker color into a scaffold-aligned rectangle border and fill the centers of the enclosed frames.

- The markers do not define freehand paths; they select a rectangle in the scaffold's boundary lattice.

references.docstring:

Input structure:

- For each object side, continue the side run outside the object, shrinking its length by two pixels per step.
- Paint every in-bounds background pixel in those shrinking continuations yellow.

- The yellow pixels are not an outline; they are the clipped extrapolated caps of each object's horizontal and vertical run profiles.

references.docstring:
Connect the blue marker to the red marker with a green shortest king-move path.

- A mostly background grid contains exactly one blue pixel and one red pixel.
- The marker pixels are separated in both row and column.

- Paint the remaining straight middle run along the longer axis, leaving the
  final diagonal step into the red pixel unpainted.

- The path is a Chebyshev-shortest route whose straight segment absorbs the
  unequal row and column distances between the two markers.

annotation.dst: single red marker pixel d
annotation.path: Chebyshev-shortest path from s toward d: diagonal steps first, then a straight run along the longer axis, with the final step diagonal into d

annotation.transform: preserve the blue/red markers and all other input pixels

references.docstring:

references.docstring:
Extract the unique filled 3x3 foreground object that uses three colors.

- The grid has a dominant background color, black/0 in the examples.
- The foreground consists of separated filled 3x3 objects.

- The selected output object is distinguished by color diversity, not by

references.docstring:

Input structure
The grid has a black background, one 8-connected red template sprite, and

pixel has the template color.

Read the control pixels left-to-right or top-to-bottom.  The copy matching
the template-color control is the original sprite; each neighboring control
becomes a same-shape copy in that control color.  The empty cells between
adjacent control pixels become the empty columns or rows between adjacent
sprite bboxes.

Key insight
The singleton control line is a compressed ordered layout: expanding each
marker to the template bbox while keeping the inter-marker gaps fixes every
copy position from the original sprite.

references.docstring:
Recolor the right-side target column-runs with the left palette colors in order.

Input structure
- The background surrounds full-height, single-color palette columns on the left

- Each target column has one contiguous vertical span, and adjacent columns with
  the same span form one rectangular run.

- Remove the palette and target marker color, leaving the background elsewhere.
- Read the palette columns from left to right.
- Recolor the target column-runs from left to right with the corresponding
  palette colors.

- The target drawing is not a connected-component problem: its visible blocks are
  the maximal adjacent column groups that share the same vertical extent.

annotation.dst: maximal target-color column-runs d on the right: adjacent columns sharing one contiguous vertical span, ordered left to right

references.docstring:

- The grid contains only blue, red, and teal pixels.
- The red pixels form one or more 4-connected objects.
- Each red object is embedded in exactly one adjacent non-red carrier color.

- Clear each red object back to its carrier color to recover the blue and teal regions.
- A red object carried by blue moves right until its bounding box touches the right edge of that blue region.
- A red object carried by teal moves left until its bounding box touches the left edge of that teal region.

- The red objects are sliders inside colored horizontal lanes; the carrier color encodes the slide direction.

references.docstring:
Erase the cross marker and add a reflected adjacent copy of the other foreground sprite.

- One foreground color forms the sprite to preserve and duplicate.

- Rotate that stem direction 90 degrees in row/column coordinates to choose the side of the sprite's bounding box.
- Mirror the sprite vertically for an above/below copy, or horizontally for a left/right copy, and paste it adjacent to that side.
- Output only the original sprite and its reflected copy; the marker is erased to background.

- The marker is not a target location: its asymmetric arm encodes which adjacent side receives the mirrored sprite.

annotation.symbol_instructions: marker's uniquely longest arm, rotated 90 degrees in row/column coordinates, selects the adjacent side

references.docstring:
Repeat each colored motif from the end of a grey ruler bar to fill the rectangle beside that bar.

A black-background grid contains one or more straight grey bars.  Each bar is
either vertical, with a colored rectangular motif attached to its lower-right
end, or horizontal, with a colored rectangular motif attached below its
left end.
Rule
For a vertical grey bar, repeat the attached motif upward/downward along the
bar's rows and paint the rectangle immediately to the bar's right.  For a
horizontal grey bar, repeat the attached motif left/right along the bar's
columns and paint the rectangle immediately below the bar.

references.docstring:

- In every row where the moving color appears, it forms one contiguous horizontal run ending at the right edge.

- Process each occupied row independently.
- Clear the moving run from the right edge.
- Repaint that run starting immediately to the right of the row's rightmost barrier pixel, or at column 0 when no barrier is present.
- Keep the barrier pixels and all rows without moving pixels unchanged.

Key insight
- The fixed pixels are row-wise stoppers; each moving run simply slides left as far as possible without crossing the nearest stopper.

  of another candidate's red pixel set.

- Recolor every other grey pixel in the selected window to orange, leaving
  red pixels and the rest of the grid unchanged.

- The red pixels identify local 3x3 foreground blocks; maximal red-set

references.docstring:
Complete the separated array of one-hole tiles.

length is n*n+n-1, partitioning it into an n by n array of n by n tiles

present; each present tile is filled with foreground except for one
background pixel at the local coordinate matching the tile's array position.

(tile row, tile column), fill that n by n tile with the foreground color and
leave only the local pixel at (tile row, tile column) as background.

the larger tile array, so the sparse input samples define the complete
position-coded pattern.

annotation.dst: empty tile slots in the same separated array
annotation.transform: complete every tile as foreground except for its coordinate-label background pixel, and keep separator rows and columns background

references.docstring:
Extend a solid rectangle into side stripes, leaving blank the rows or columns marked by control pixels.

Input structure:
- The background is the dominant color.

- Keep the original rectangle and markers unchanged.
- Above and below the rectangle, fill each rectangle column that has no marker on that side.
- Left and right of the rectangle, fill each rectangle row that has no marker on that side.

Key insight:
- The markers encode the excluded projected rows or columns for their side of the rectangle; the unmarked positions become rectangle-colored extension stripes.

annotation.transform: extend the rectangle color through every unmarked projected row or column on each side; marker-aligned rows or columns stay bg and the markers are preserved

references.docstring:
Fill the black target rectangle with a left-right mirror of the colored source motif.

Input structure:
- A dominant background surrounds one fully occupied colored rectangular motif.
- A single black rectangular region is the same shape as the colored motif.

Rule:
- Crop the colored motif from its tight bounding box.
- Reflect that crop horizontally and paste it over the black rectangle.

Key insight:
- The black region is not erased by a fill color; it is a destination slot for the mirrored motif.

annotation.dst: black rectangular slot d
annotation.match_cond: unique s maps to unique d; s.bbox.shape == d.bbox.shape

references.docstring:
Paint a blue 3x3 hollow neighborhood around each red marker inside a green object's bounding rectangle.

- The input contains a black background, green 4-connected objects, and red marker pixels.
- Each green object forms an almost-rectangular region; its bounding box identifies the region it controls.
- The active red markers are exactly the red pixels lying inside one of those green-object bounding boxes.

- For each active red marker, recolor all in-bounds 8-neighbor cells to blue.
- If two active markers touch, their marker centers remain red rather than being overwritten by the other's blue stamp.

- Red pixels outside the green rectangles are distractors; containment in a green component's bbox selects the markers to stamp.

annotation.transform: paint each selected marker's in-bounds 8-neighborhood blue, except selected marker centers remain red; pixels outside all stamps stay unchanged

references.docstring:
Complete same-color marker segments inside a regular lattice of framed tiles.

Input structure
- The grid is partitioned by separator rows and columns into 4x4 framed tiles.
- All tile borders have one frame color, and each 2x2 tile interior has a dominant fill color.
- Other interior colors are endpoint markers, with their exact 2x2 subcell position preserved.

- When two or more endpoints in a group share a tile row, fill every intervening tile at that same subcell with the marker color.
- When two or more endpoints in a group share a tile column, fill every intervening tile at that same subcell with the marker color.

Key insight
- The colored endpoints are not connected in pixel space; they are connected on the coarser tile lattice, and the chosen interior subcell identifies which lane to paint.

annotation.match_cond: markers connect only when they have the same color and the same relative interior subcell
annotation.path: straight horizontal or vertical segment on the tile lattice between matching markers that share a tile row or tile column
annotation.trajectory: paint that same relative interior subcell of every intervening tile with the marker color
annotation.transform: keep separator lines, tile frames, structural interior fill cells, and original markers unchanged

references.docstring:

- The grid contains black background and one complete one-cell-thick grey square frame.
- The frame interior and any exterior padding are black.

- Preserve the frame bbox and recolor every cell in it by its distance from the frame border.
- Shell depths repeat the color cycle grey, red, grey, black while moving inward.

references.docstring:
Extract and stack the contents between each row-aligned pair of 2x2 marker blocks.

references.docstring:
Slide closed foreground objects upward and open foreground objects downward, keeping their columns and stacking on collision.

- The remaining objects are open line-like sprites with no enclosed hole.

- Redraw every object on an empty background canvas without changing its color, shape, or horizontal position.

- A marker on a horizontal red line emits a vertical blue line through its center column; a marker on a vertical red line emits a horizontal blue line through its center row.

references.docstring:

references.docstring:
Fill black gaps with the unique known color from each cell's horizontal/vertical mirror orbit.

Input structure

references.docstring:

- For each band intersection, write the unique majority color of that input

- The output is a coarse color map of the block lattice; the internal shape

references.docstring:
Use the matching pair of tiles in each band as a color-substitution example and apply it to the remaining tile.

Stretch the compact colored line prototype onto the sparse yellow skeleton canvas.

- Treat endpoints, corners, and crossings of the prototype foreground as graph vertices.

- The endpoints are connected by one shortest 4-neighbor route through non-blue cells.

- Keep every original cell unchanged.
- Find the unique shortest 4-neighbor path from one red endpoint to the other while treating blue cells as blocked.
- Recolor only the black interior cells of that path to yellow.

- The blue cells form maze walls, and the output is the single shortest corridor between the two red endpoints.

annotation.dst: the other red endpoint d
annotation.path: unique shortest 4-neighbor route from s to d through background cells, treating blue cells as blockers

references.docstring:
Separate four overlapping-looking copies of one 2x2 sprite into the four corners of a 5x5 canvas.

foreground pixels without overlap, then stamp that mask into the upper-left,

The tangled input arrangement is only a compact packing of four identical
small sprites; the output regularizes the packing by inserting a blank middle

annotation.dst: four separated 2x2 corner slots in a 5x5 output

references.docstring:

Recolor each grey diagonal band by extending the horizontal marker palette through its diagonal layers.

Input structure

- Keep the background and marker pixels unchanged.
- For each grey band, normalize its slant so the top cap begins at local

- The visible grey bands are diagonal ribbons; their color pattern is not
  row-wise but layered from the seed end, with the far cap clipped so the

Stamp the compact upper template into every marked lower mask cell as an expanded block image.

- Below it is a same-size mask containing only background and red marker pixels.

annotation.symbol_instructions: upper template region encodes the 3x3 tile; lower red mask encodes the coarse output positions that receive the tile

references.docstring:
Summarize each foreground color as a top-aligned vertical bar ordered by bbox height.

Input structure
The grid has a dominant background color and several foreground color masks.

the top cells of that column with the color for its measured height.

The input positions and horizontal extents are discarded; only each color's
vertical span determines the histogram height and column order.

annotation.match_cond: rank(s) == rank(d)
annotation.transform: fill each column with s.color for s.bbox.height cells from the top, leaving the rest as background
annotation.grid_shape: height is the largest foreground color bbox height; width is the number of foreground colors

references.docstring:
Pack all foreground fragments into a solid compact rectangle while preserving their colors.

- Sort fragments by decreasing area, with equal-area fragments ordered left-to-right in the input.
- For each fragment, try its identity/reflected/rotated orientations in that order and scan placements from top-left to bottom-right.

The scattered objects are jigsaw fragments; the output is their canonical top-left packing into the smallest near-square rectangle.

annotation.dst: compact 3x4 rectangle packed from top-left to bottom-right

- A background lattice of separated framed tiles; the frame color is the unique most frequent non-background color.
- Each tile region contains one solid non-frame interior block.

- For each marker color, find its two row bands and two column bands.
- Paint that color through background cells along the two horizontal and two vertical sides of the implied rectangle.
- Preserve all original frame, default interior, marker, and off-path background pixels.

Key insight
- The repeated tile frames define which cells are obstacles and which cells are background channels; matching interior colors supply rectangle corners independent of tile and marker size.

annotation.dst: same-color marker blocks sharing a marker row band or column band
annotation.path: for each marker color, connect the four corner blocks along the two horizontal and two vertical sides of their implied rectangle, crossing only background channel cells
annotation.trajectory: paint every background cell on each rectangle side with the marker color
annotation.transform: keep all framed tiles, default interiors, marker blocks, and off-path background unchanged

references.docstring:
Fill the inside of a rectangular frame with alternating red and yellow square rings around its inner control pixel.

Input structure
- The grid has one background color and one foreground color.
- The foreground forms a rectangular one-pixel-thick frame.
- Exactly one foreground control pixel lies inside the frame.

Rule
- Preserve the frame and the control pixel.
- For each background pixel inside the frame, compute its Chebyshev distance
  from the control pixel.
- Odd distances become yellow; even distances become red.

Key insight
- The added colors are concentric square rings centered on the lone interior
  control pixel, with ring color determined by distance parity.

annotation.transform: preserve the frame and control pixel; recolor each background interior pixel by Chebyshev-distance parity from the control pixel, odd to yellow and even to red

references.docstring:

- Marker colors are green, pink, orange, and teal; orange markers on the lower border are terminal when hit from above.

- Start with a horizontal red ray from the red edge pixel.

- Process emitted rows/columns depth-first, with right/down emissions taking priority over left/up emissions when both are discovered together.
- If a downward vertical ray reaches an orange marker on the lower border, stop there without opening a new horizontal ray.

references.docstring:

references.docstring:

references.docstring:
Complete each partial copy of the yellow-marked 3x3 template by adding the template's yellow cells.

Input structure
- A black background contains scattered blue/teal distractors and one full 3x3 sprite whose yellow pixels mark the cells to add.

references.docstring:

- The side panels share one background color.

references.docstring:

Input structure

- The examples use a 4x4 tile and produce a same-height strip five tiles wide.

- Concatenate five whole-tile blocks across columns.
- Use the original tile in blocks 1, 3, and 5.
- Use the left-right mirror of the tile in blocks 2 and 4.

annotation.dst: five horizontal tile slots in the output strip

references.docstring:
Draw the straight segment between the two red markers, turning crossed blue pixels green and crossed empty pixels red.

Input structure
- The input contains only black background, blue foreground pixels, and exactly two red marker pixels.
- The two red markers lie on one horizontal, vertical, or 45-degree diagonal line.

- Copy the input grid.
- Walk the inclusive straight segment from one red marker to the other.
- Each path cell that was blue becomes green; each path cell that was black or red becomes red.

references.docstring:

A black-background grid contains exactly two foreground colors: one color forms a single prototype object, and the other forms multiple candidate objects.

The prototype is a line-drawing symbol; candidate symbols can be stretched in row/column runs, so matching must compare the compressed topology rather than raw size.

references.docstring:
Return the corner tile mask that is missing from the rotation family shown in the input.

Input structure
- The grid is an odd-sized square split by a one-pixel background cross into four square corner tiles.
- Three corner tiles contain masks made from one source color on the background.
- The remaining corner tile is a solid non-background placeholder color.

- Read the three source masks from the corner tiles.
- Generate the four rotations of that mask family.
- Output the unique rotated mask that is not one of the three source masks, using the source color on the background.

Key insight
The placeholder marks the missing fourth member of a rotation set; the answer is that absent tile, not the placeholder itself.

annotation.dst: the tile-size output for the solid placeholder corner

references.docstring:
Fill the interior implied by a left half-outline and its horizontal mirror.

Input structure
A 2D grid contains one background color and one foreground color. The
foreground is the left half of a horizontally symmetric closed outline, with
its global right edge immediately left of the vertical symmetry axis.

Rule
Clear the outline. For each row containing foreground, take the foreground
pixel closest to the axis as the left boundary, mirror it across the
half-column axis just to the right of the global right edge, and fill only
the cells strictly between those two boundary pixels.

Key insight
Row segments near the top and bottom are outline, not fill; the row's
rightmost foreground pixel is the inner boundary that determines that row's
hidden symmetric interior span.

annotation.dst: interior of the completed horizontally symmetric outline on the same canvas
annotation.transform: erase the visible outline; for each foreground row, mirror the row's rightmost foreground pixel across the half-column axis and fill the cells strictly between the boundary pair with the same color

references.docstring:
Return the hollow 3x3 sprite that is enclosed by the sparse guide mask.

Input structure
- The background is the dominant color.
- Several monochrome 3x3 hollow-square sprites sit on the background.
- The remaining foreground pixels are a single-color sparse guide mask whose bbox frames one sprite.

Rule
- Find every hollow 3x3 square sprite.
- Build the guide mask from all non-background pixels that are not part of those sprites.
- Return the tight bbox crop of the unique sprite fully contained in the guide mask bbox.

- The guide pixels do not draw the output; their bounding rectangle selects which existing hollow-square sprite to crop.

annotation.dst: sparse guide-mask bbox d
annotation.match_cond: s.bbox is fully contained in d.bbox
annotation.transform: return the tight bbox crop of matched s
annotation.grid_shape: 3x3 crop

references.docstring:
Connect all red control pixels by drawing green orthogonal segments to the unique red spine.

Input structure
- A black background contains only red control pixels.
- Exactly two red pixels share one row or one column; this aligned pair defines the spine segment.
- Every other red pixel lies within the span of that spine along the perpendicular direction.

Rule
- Paint the background cells between the aligned red pair green, preserving the red endpoints.
- If the spine is horizontal, draw a vertical green segment from each other red pixel to the spine.
- If the spine is vertical, draw a horizontal green segment from each other red pixel to the spine.

Key insight
- The only repeated row or column among the red pixels is the connector trunk; all remaining pixels attach to it perpendicularly.

annotation.path: paint the spine between the aligned red pair, then cast each remaining red pixel perpendicularly to the spine along its row or column

references.docstring:
Rotate the red segment one quarter-turn clockwise around the grey marker, recoloring its original cells green.

Input structure:
- The grid has a dominant background, exactly one grey marker, and one red

- The red segment is a straight horizontal or vertical bar attached to the

- The clockwise-rotated red segment fits on the same canvas.

- Locate the grey marker and the adjacent red cell, which gives the bar's

- Recolor every input red cell green.
- Draw a red segment of the same length from the marker in the direction
  obtained by rotating the original direction clockwise.

references.docstring:
Expand the centered red pixel into a square red V with a periodic blue diagonal fill.

Input structure
- The input is a single odd-length row with black background.
- Exactly one foreground pixel is present, and it is red at the center column.

- Create an N x N background canvas, where N is the input width.
- Draw red diagonals from the top-center marker down-left and down-right until they hit the side edges.
- Paint blue on the NW-SE diagonal lattice with the marker column's modulo-4 phase, clipped to the strict interior of the red V above the midpoint and unclipped below it.

- The lone red pixel is the apex of a triangular pattern; the blue cells are one repeated diagonal family inside and below that triangle.

references.docstring:
Extract the unique partition cell whose foreground pixels are all one color.

Input structure
- A black-background square grid is divided by full horizontal and vertical

- Most cells contain scattered foreground noise of several colors.
- Exactly one cell has non-background pixels of a single color only.

- Ignore the separator lines and split the grid into its equal cells.

- The answer is not built from the whole grid; it is the only separator-free

references.docstring:
Complete the dominant-color object by adding its left-right mirror image.

Input structure
A rectangular grid contains one uniquely most frequent color forming the main
foreground object, with other colors acting as clutter/noise.

Reflect every pixel of the dominant color across the vertical centerline of
the grid and recolor the reflected cells with that same dominant color.

dominant-color mask horizontally symmetric.

references.docstring:
Build a 3x3 mosaic of whole-grid mirror reflections around the original tile.

- The input is a 3x3 color grid; every cell belongs to the source tile.

Rule
- Produce a 9x9 grid split into nine 3x3 tile slots.
- The center slot is the original tile.
- Slots above or below the center reverse source rows.
- Slots left or right of the center reverse source columns.
- Corner slots reverse both rows and columns.

The output is reflection wallpaper of the entire small grid, not per-pixel scaling or color-specific processing.

annotation.dst: 3x3 array of 3x3 tile slots in the output

references.docstring:
Erase the control bars and tile each matched sprite toward its bar.

Input structure
- The background contains colored non-line sprites plus one-cell-thick control

- A horizontal bar has the same column span as a sprite; a vertical bar has
  the same row span as a sprite.

Rule
- Remove every control bar.
- For each bar, find the nearest sprite aligned with the bar's span on the
  perpendicular axis.
- Repeat that sprite periodically from its original position toward the bar,
  clipping at the grid boundary and leaving sprite-background cells empty.

- The bar is not copied itself; it gives the direction and terminal line for

annotation.trajectory: copy s every full sprite height/width along the path, clipping at grid edges and treating background cells inside s as transparent

references.docstring:
Render the lower grey slot array by replacing each colored control pixel with the matching legend template.

Input structure
A background grid has a top legend: each colored marker sits one row above and one column left of a
2x2 template drawn in a shared template ink color.  Below it is a rectangular array of 2x2 grey slots,
where a slot may contain one colored control pixel in place of grey.

Read the legend as color -> 2x2 template mask.  Convert the lower slot array into a compact array with
the same row/column layout and one background separator row/column between neighboring tiles.  Empty

annotation.dst: top legend 2x2 template masks d
annotation.match_cond: s.color == d.marker_color
annotation.transform: replace each lower slot with d.mask recolored to s.color in the compact output lattice; slots without a control pixel become background

references.docstring:
Rebuild the visible frame fragments as centered concentric square rings.

Input structure
The input has a dominant background and several non-background colors. Each
foreground color marks one square frame or center block, possibly with gaps
caused by overlap with other frames. The intended side length of a color is
the larger side of the bbox of all pixels of that color.

Rule
Sort the colors by intended side length from largest to smallest. Create a
square output whose side is the largest length, then draw each color as the
border of the centered square with that side length.

Key insight
Positions in the input are only a scrambled/overlapped display of the
nested frames; the bbox side lengths provide the layer order and output
ring sizes.

annotation.dst: centered square frame layers d ordered from outermost to innermost
annotation.match_cond: rank(s by decreasing side length) == rank(d from outside inward)
annotation.transform: draw each s.color as the one-cell border of its matched centered square
annotation.grid_shape: square side length is the largest source bbox side length

references.docstring:

- The input is a two-dimensional grid containing a repeated rectangular color tile.
- Black pixels are holes in that wallpaper, not part of the tile.
- Every tile phase is visible at least once in a non-black cell.

- Find the unique smallest row and column period whose non-black cells agree by repeated phase.
- Reconstruct the full grid by writing the tile color at each cell's phase.

- The corrupted cells are exactly the black pixels; their colors are determined by the repeated phase shared with non-black copies elsewhere.

references.docstring:

Input structure
- The background is black.
- Each foreground color represents one object: either a filled rectangle, possibly partly hidden by another color, or a filled rectangle with a straight one-cell-thick tail of length at least two.

- Restore every non-slider object as the filled rectangle of its input bounding box.
- For every slider, discard the tail and translate only the rectangular body by the tail length in the tail direction.
- Draw the translated slider rectangles over the restored static rectangles.

- A thin tail is a displacement vector for its rectangle, while wider missing areas inside another color's bounding box are occlusion that should be restored.

annotation.trajectory: move only the solid rectangular body to its final translated bbox; do not leave a trail

references.docstring:
Recolor each grey placeholder pixel with the visible control color in its row.

- Preserve background and control pixels.

- The grey shape is not filled as a connected object; the row-aligned control marker supplies the replacement color independently for every grey pixel in that row.

annotation.transform: replace each grey pixel with the color of the control pixel in the same row; preserve background and control pixels
annotation.symbol_instructions: marker-column control pixels give the replacement color for grey pixels in their row

references.docstring:
Extend the top colored columns downward, routing blocked columns around horizontal obstacle segments.

Input structure
The background is the dominant color.  Row 0 contains a single non-background
source color forming vertical columns at the top.  The remaining foreground
color appears only as one row of horizontal obstacle segments below those
columns.

Copy the input, then extend every source column to the bottom of the grid.

column.  Exact midpoint ties detour to the right side.

teal columns to the closest free side before the columns continue downward.

annotation.trajectory: paint the falling and sliding trail with teal
annotation.transform: preserve the red obstacle segments and existing teal pixels

references.docstring:

Return a 3x3 background grid with the first N cells in row-major order set to the marker color, where N is the number of marker pixels strictly inside the frame.

references.docstring:

- The foreground color may appear in one or more cells.

annotation.dst: 3-by-3 array of input-sized tile slots

references.docstring:
Paint a teal diamond envelope around each straight foreground bar.

Input structure
- The grid has a single background color and one non-background foreground color.

- For a horizontal bar, paint teal rows above and below it; each step away from the bar shortens the interval by one pixel at both ends.

- A bar of length L defines a centered diamond of radius floor((L - 1) / 2), with the original bar forming the middle line and teal filling only the surrounding background cells.

references.docstring:

references.docstring:

A same-size grid contains an otherwise regular two-dimensional color lattice, with black rectangles masking some cells.

The visible cells still include every residue of the repeating tile, so the black pixels are occlusions rather than objects to preserve.

references.docstring:

references.docstring:

references.docstring:

references.docstring:

The grid has a dominant background color, and every foreground cell lies in
the leftmost column.  The foreground colors are teal, red, yellow, and

same row at its fixed color lane: teal in column 1, red in column 2, yellow

The color is preserved and acts as the horizontal lane code, so all

references.docstring:
Extract the only connected foreground sprite whose exact colored crop appears twice in the input.

Input structure:
- The background is the most common color.
- Foreground cells form several separated 4-connected multicolor sprites.
- Exactly one sprite pattern, including background holes inside its bbox, occurs twice.

- Crop each foreground sprite to its tight bounding box.
- Compare the full colored crops, preserving internal background cells.

Copy the foreground source mask from its singleton anchor control pixel to every destination control pixel.

- A background grid contains a multi-pixel source mask color and control pixels in other colors.
- One singleton control pixel is the anchor; its 4-neighborhood has the strongest contact with the source mask color.
- All other non-background, non-source control pixels are destination markers.

- Replace the whole scene with background, then stamp that relative mask in the source color at each destination marker.

- The controls mark origins: the singleton anchor gives the source mask's coordinate frame, and the other control pixels are target origins for copied masks.

references.docstring:

- The grid contains exactly two visible pattern colors plus pink marker pixels.
- Ignoring the pink cells, all visible pixels are consistent with one smallest rectangular repeating tile.

- Treat pink pixels as missing values.
- Infer the unique minimum-area row/column period whose residues all have a single visible color.

The pink pixels are occlusions in a global periodic tile, not independent objects.

references.docstring:
Collapse the scattered non-guide pixels orthogonally onto the cells immediately beside the straight guide bar.

Input structure
- The background is the dominant color.
- One non-background color forms a one-cell-thick horizontal or vertical guide bar, possibly with gaps along the bar axis.
- The only other non-background color appears as isolated source pixels scattered on either side of the guide.

Rule
- Start from an otherwise empty background canvas and keep the guide bar fixed.
- If the guide is horizontal, each source pixel whose column contains a guide pixel moves to the row directly above or below that guide pixel, preserving its side of the guide.
- If the guide is vertical, each source pixel whose row contains a guide pixel moves to the column directly left or right of that guide pixel, preserving its side of the guide.
- Source pixels whose perpendicular projection would hit a gap in the guide are erased.

Key insight
- The guide bar defines the valid landing slots; the scattered pixels are not copied in place, but compressed along perpendicular sightlines to the nearest cells beside that guide.

references.docstring:
Extend each green plus outward as row and column rays in its center color.

Input structure
- The background is the dominant color.
- Every foreground pixel belongs to a green four-arm plus frame.
- Each plus center is either a marker color or the background color.

- From each plus, paint horizontal rays in the center color from just beyond

- A background-colored plus is still an emitter: its vertical ray clears

references.docstring:
Trace the edge marker inward through broken wall segments, branching at each segment opening.

and one other foreground color forming parallel, broken wall segments.

the next cell is a wall, paint the near side of that contiguous wall segment
plus its adjacent openings, then continue inward from every in-bounds opening.

Key insight
The output is not a flood fill: each obstacle is handled as the single wall
segment directly hit by the current ray, whose endpoints determine the next

references.docstring:

Input structure:
- A square grid contains one occluding color whose pixels are not part of the final design.

- Infer the occluding color as the only color whose removal gives conflict-free high-evidence row and column reflection axes.
- Fill occluding pixels from the unique visible color in their horizontal, vertical, and 180-degree reflection orbit.
- Fill any remaining occluding pixels from the unique visible color at a 90-degree quarter-turn counterpart.

Key insight:
- The maroon pixels are damage over a shifted kaleidoscope-like pattern; the hidden color is determined by a visible mate in the same symmetry orbit.

references.docstring:
